'''Sheldon "Shelly" Schultz''' (January 21, 1933 – January 31, 2017) was an American physicist, who was a professor at [[University of California, San Diego]]. Best known for his contributions to the discovery of [[metamaterials]] and [[Negative-index metamaterial|negative-index media]], he served as the Director of the Center for Magnetic Recording Research at UCSD from 1990 to 2000.

==Biography==
Sheldon Schultz was born on January 21, 1933 in [[New York City]]. A graduate of [[Stuyvesant High School]], he received [[bachelor's degree]] in [[mechanical engineering]] from [[Stevens Institute of Technology]] in 1954. He pursued his doctoral studies in physics at [[Columbia University]] under the supervision of [[Polykarp Kusch]] and William Lichten, receiving his Ph.D. degree in 1960. In the same year, he joined the Department of Physics at [[University of California, San Diego]] as one of the founding faculty members.<ref name="obituary-aip"/> Having received a [[Sloan Research Fellowship]] in 1964, he became a full professor in 1971 and continued as a research professor until 2013.<ref name="ucsd"/> He also served as the Director of the Center for Magnetic Recording Research at UCSD from 1990 to 2000. He died at his home in [[La Jolla]] on January 31, 2017 from complications due to [[Parkinson's disease]], being survived by his wife, three children and grandchildren. He was a Fellow of the IEEE and [[American Physical Society]], and was the president of the [[nanotechnology]] company, Seashell Technology LLC.<ref name="obituary-aip"/> 

Schultz is best known for his work on [[metamaterials]] and [[Negative-index metamaterial|negative-index of refraction]],<ref name="obituary-aip"/>  which he and his research group have demonstrated experimentally in 2000 for [[microwave]] frequencies.<ref name="science"/><ref name="physics-today"/><ref name="smith2000"/> His work on metamaterials, though controversial at the time, was listed as "Top Ten Breakthroughs in 2003" by journal ''[[Science (journal)|Science]]'' and one of these publications was selected among "PRL Milestones" by ''[[Physical Review Letters]]''.<ref name="obituary-aip"/> In 2009, he was included in the [[Clarivate Citation Laureates]] list of potential future winners of the [[Nobel Prize in Physics]] along with and [[John Pendry]] and [[David R. Smith (physicist)|David R. Smith]], latter of whom was a post-doctoral researcher in Schultz's group.<ref name="reuters"/> His other work included the design and fabrication of subwavelength [[Antenna (radio)|antenna]]s, [[localized surface plasmon]]-based optical [[transducer]]s for biochemical and medical applications, and Kerr [[Near-field scanning optical microscope|near-field scanning optical microscopy]], as well as applications of magnetic field–modulated [[microwave spectroscopy]] and [[electron paramagnetic resonance]].<ref name="obituary-aip"/><ref name="ucsd"/>
